Javan
jā'van
n. (fourth son of Japheth; in prophetic usage the Greek world, Ionia and the seafaring west)
From Hebrew Yavan, the name behind Ionia — the Greek-speaking coastlands of Asia Minor and the Aegean. The Septuagint renders it Hellas, and the prophets use it for Greece.

Biblical Definition

Javan stands fourth among the sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2), and his own sons — Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, Dodanim — spread out into the sea-lanes: “By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands” (Gen 10:5). What makes Javan more than a name in a list is what the prophets do with it. Ezekiel puts him in the great lament over Tyre as one of the merchant peoples: “Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market” (Eze 27:13) — a trade in men, named as such, centuries before any modern conscience discovered the evil. Daniel sees the same people as an empire on the horizon, the rough goat from the west whose great horn is broken and replaced by four (Dan 8:21-22). And Isaiah, in the closing vision of the book, sends survivors of the LORD's judgment out to the far nations — “to Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame” — that they may declare His glory among the Gentiles (Isa 66:19). The line runs straight from a genealogy to a missionary commission: the Greek world named in Genesis is the world Paul will walk, and the tongue of Javan is the tongue the New Testament is written in.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Javan; in sacred geography he is a son of Japheth and the head of the Ionian or Greek nations.

expand to see more

JAVAN, n. The fourth son of Japheth, and father of the Ionian or Grecian people.

His sons were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim, who peopled the isles and coasts of the Mediterranean.

The prophets use the name for Greece, and the Greek version renders it Hellas.

Javan is named among the merchants of Tyre, trading in men and vessels of brass.

In Daniel the kingdom of Javan is the Grecian empire that succeeded the Persian.

Key Scripture

Gen 10:2 — "The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras."

Gen 10:4 — "And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim."

Eze 27:13 — "Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market."

Isa 66:19 — "And I will set a sign among them, and I will send those that escape of them unto the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow, to Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame, neither have seen my glory; and they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles."

Modern Corruption

Daniel's Greek prophecy is routinely redated after the fact so that it predicts nothing, and Ezekiel's plain naming of a slave trade is passed over as though ancient traffic in persons were morally invisible.

expand to see more

Daniel 8 names the kingdom of Javan, describes its rise from the west, breaks its great horn at the height of its strength, and divides it four ways. Because that is what happened to Alexander, the standard critical move is to date the book after the events and call the prophecy a record. The dictionary rejects the redating and holds a sixth-century Daniel, for the plain reason that the book presents itself as prophecy and the Lord Jesus cites Daniel as a prophet (Mat 24:15). A method that converts every fulfilled prediction into late composition has not examined the evidence; it has adopted a rule that no prediction may be admitted, and then found what the rule requires.

The second corruption is a silence. Ezekiel says the merchants of Javan “traded the persons of men”, and it is common to read past that clause as commercial background. Scripture does not read past it. The Mosaic law made the stealing and selling of a man a capital crime — “he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16) — and Paul places menstealers in the same list as murderers and perjurers as things contrary to sound doctrine (1Ti 1:10). The trade in image-bearers is named as sin by the God who made them, in the ancient world and in every world since; the honour of the prophets is that they wrote it down while it was still respectable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yavan (H3120), Javan, Ionia, Greece; 'iy (H339), isle; rakal (H7402), to trade, traffick; Greek Hellas (G1671), Greece.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yavan (H3120) — Javan; the son of Japheth, and by extension Ionia and the Greek world.

Hebrew 'iy (H339) — isle, coastland; the habitat assigned to Javan's sons in Gen 10:5.

Hebrew rakal (H7402) — to travel for trade, to traffick; the merchant word of Eze 27.

Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul, person; “the persons of men” whom Javan sold.

Greek Hellas (G1671) — Greece; the Septuagint's rendering of Javan and the New Testament's name for the land.

Usage

"“The sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim” — a genealogy that is also a map of the sea."

"“They traded the persons of men” — the prophet names the traffic without euphemism."

"“To Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off” — the Greek world marked for the gospel from Isaiah forward."
